label: Rank, Submersions, Immersions, Embeddings
notes: This chapter, printed pages 77 through 97, asks a single guiding question: when can a nonlinear smooth map be trusted to look like a linear map after we choose the right coordinates near a point? The answer is governed entirely by the rank of the differential, and the three full-rank cases organize everything that follows.

label: The Rank of a Smooth Map
notes: The rank of a map at a point is just the rank of its differential there, computed as the rank of any coordinate Jacobian. Because rank is a linear-algebra invariant under change of basis, it is the first diagnostic we apply, and it is lower semicontinuous, so full rank persists on an open set.

label: Full Rank Is an Open Condition
notes: A nonzero minor of size equal to the rank is a continuous function, so wherever the differential has full rank it keeps full rank nearby. This is why being a submersion or an immersion is a local, open condition. The four panels separate genuine full-rank behaviour from rank that drops along a curve or a line.

label: The Rank Theorem
notes: The rank theorem is the chapter's central normal form. If a smooth map has constant rank near a point, suitable charts on source and target turn it into the linear projection that keeps the first r coordinates and zeroes the rest. Emphasize that the hypothesis is constant rank, not merely full rank at a single point.

label: Inverse Function Theorem
notes: The square full-rank case is the inverse function theorem: an invertible differential gives a smooth local inverse, so the map is a local diffeomorphism. Walk through the triangular example whose Jacobian determinant is one everywhere, making the inverse an explicit polynomial with zero residual on the grid.

label: Immersions
notes: An immersion has injective differential everywhere, so no tangent direction is crushed. The rank theorem specializes to say an immersion locally looks like the standard inclusion of a coordinate plane. Stress that this is purely local: a single regular curve immerses the line, yet its global image can still misbehave.

label: Submersions and Local Sections
notes: A submersion has surjective differential everywhere and locally looks like a projection. The rank theorem produces a smooth local section through every point, a right inverse of the map. Local sections are the engine behind nearly every structural property of submersions that we prove in the rest of the chapter.

label: Submersions Are Open Maps
notes: Because each point sits in the image of a local section, a submersion sends open sets to open sets. A surjective submersion is therefore a quotient map, and a map out of the base is smooth exactly when its composite with the submersion is smooth. This is the characteristic property used to pass smoothly to quotients.

label: Smooth Embeddings
notes: An embedding is an immersion that is also a homeomorphism onto its image with the subspace topology. The differential only sees infinitesimal data, so injectivity of the differential is not enough; we additionally need the image topology to match the domain. Embeddings are the maps that realize one manifold faithfully inside another.

label: Immersion That Is Not an Embedding
notes: The figure-eight curve is the canonical counterexample: a smooth injective immersion of an open interval whose two ends approach the crossing point, so the image topology disagrees with the domain. Contrast it with the embedded arc on the right, and mention the dense irrational line on the torus as a second failure.

label: Submersions and Level Sets
notes: A scalar map is a submersion exactly where its gradient is nonzero, and there its level sets are regular. The unit circle is a regular level of the squared norm, while the crossing locus of xy equals zero is singular at the origin because both partials vanish there. Rank gives an immediate regular-value test.

label: Smooth Covering Maps
notes: A smooth covering map is a local diffeomorphism whose sheets repeat over evenly covered neighborhoods. The exponential cover of the circle lifts a small arc to disjoint intervals in the line; picking one sheet gives a smooth local section that is unique once the lifted base point is fixed. Proper local diffeomorphisms are coverings.

label: Proof Traffic and Takeaways
notes: Trace the dependency: the inverse function theorem feeds the rank theorem, which yields normal forms for immersions and submersions, then local sections, openness, quotient behaviour, and coverings. The recurring moral is that rank is the coordinate-free invariant, constant rank is the hypothesis that straightens the map, and topology supplies what the differential cannot see.
